# RAG Evaluation: Academic Benchmarks and Production Practice

## 1. TL;DR

RAG evaluation has split into two converging tracks: academic benchmarks (RAGAS, RGB, ARES, CRUD-RAG, RAGChecker, MIRAGE) that emphasize standardized, often reference-based datasets and fine-grained diagnostic metrics [2][4][5][9][11], and production workflows (LangChain/LangSmith, LlamaIndex, TruLens, DeepEval) that favor small curated Q&A sets, reference-free LLM-as-judge scoring, and CI/CD integration [14][15][17][19][20]. RAGAS is the clearest bridge — academic in origin, widely adopted in production [4][15][16][19] — while the two worlds still diverge on dataset scale, metric philosophy (BLEU-style reference matching vs. faithfulness scoring), and where evaluation lives in the development lifecycle [13][17][20]. Caveat: rate-limiting on arXiv/Semantic Scholar left several benchmark-level specifics (ARES, CRUD-RAG) unverified; treat those claims as provisional.

## 2. Key papers

- **Introduction to Information Retrieval (2009)** — Foundational IR text underpinning retrieval-quality metrics (precision, recall, MAP, nDCG) reused in RAG eval — https://doi.org/10.5860/choice.46-2715 [1]
- **Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey (2023)** — Widely cited survey framing RAG architectures and evaluation dimensions — https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2312.10997 [2]
- **RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation (2024)** — Reference-free, LLM-based metrics (faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision/recall); the academic-to-production bridge — https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2024.eacl-demo.16 [4]
- **Benchmarking Large Language Models in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (2024)** — The RGB benchmark; hallucination- and noise-robustness-focused evaluation of RAG — https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v38i16.29728 [5]
- **Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering (2020)** — Canonical retriever baseline whose evaluation protocol (top-k recall, EM/F1) still anchors retrieval-side RAG eval — https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2020.emnlp-main.550 [7]
- **Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine (2024)** — Domain-specific RAG benchmark showing general-purpose metrics miss clinical failure modes — https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2024.findings-acl.372 [8]
- **RAGChecker: A Fine-grained Framework for Diagnosing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (2024)** — Decomposes end-to-end scores into claim-level retrieval and generation diagnostics — https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2408.08067 [9]
- **MIRAGE: A Metric-Intensive Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation (2025)** — Pushes toward multi-metric, fine-grained evaluation beyond single-score leaderboards — https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.findings-naacl.157 [11]
- **RAG-RewardBench: Benchmarking Reward Models in Retrieval Augmented Generation for Preference Alignment (2025)** — Evaluates reward models for RAG preference alignment, connecting eval to training signals — https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.findings-acl.877 [12]
- **Design and Performance Evaluation of LLM-Based RAG Pipelines for Chatbot Services in International Student Admissions (2025)** — Applied production-style evaluation of a deployed RAG pipeline — https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics14153095 [10]
- **The Multimodal Brain Tumor Image Segmentation Benchmark (BRATS) (2014)** — Included in the source set; serves as a methodological precedent for standardized, community benchmark design rather than a RAG-specific work — https://doi.org/10.1109/tmi.2014.2377694 [3]
- **Affordance-Compiled Intelligence: Observable-Only Cognitive Impedance Matching for No-Meta LLM-Integrated Systems (2020)** — Listed in the source set; not a RAG evaluation benchmark — flag as likely mis-attributed and verify before citing — https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2005.11401 [6]

## 3. Datasets

No datasets were confirmed from the retrieval pass. Named benchmarks (RGB, CRUD-RAG, MIRAGE, RAG-RewardBench, medical RAG) imply associated datasets [5][8][11][12], but their identifiers, sizes, and licenses were not verified due to API rate-limiting. Do not cite dataset specifics until primary sources are checked.

## 4. Suggested next steps

1. **Verify the unconfirmed benchmarks directly.** Pull ARES, CRUD-RAG, and the 2025 survey (arXiv 2407.13193) from primary sources to confirm metric definitions, dataset composition, and citation counts; the current synthesis flags these as provisional.
2. **Build a metric-to-dataset mapping table.** For each confirmed benchmark (RAGAS, RGB, RAGChecker, MIRAGE, RAG-RewardBench, medical RAG), record: retrieval metrics, generation metrics, reference-based vs. reference-free, dataset size, domain, and license [4][5][8][9][11][12]. This closes the "datasets found: none" gap.
3. **Reconcile academic vs. production metric vocabularies.** Produce a crosswalk between academic terms (context relevance, groundedness, answer correctness) and production tooling terms (RAGAS faithfulness, TruLens groundedness, DeepEval answer relevancy) to expose where the same concept is measured differently [13][15][16][17][19].
4. **Run a small empirical comparison.** Take one production-style curated Q&A set and score it with RAGAS, DeepEval, and TruLens on the same pipeline; report inter-tool agreement [14][15][17][19][20]. This tests the synthesis claim that production converges on reference-free faithfulness scoring and would surface any divergence the literature review missed.

# Research Report: Datasets and Benchmarks for Evaluating LLM Agent Tool Use

## 1. TL;DR

Evidence collection for this survey was severely constrained — arXiv and Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 429/503 errors across nearly all subagents, and Hugging Face / Papers with Code yielded almost no benchmark datasets. As a result, only **BFCL (Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard)** has verified live adoption evidence, while **AgentBench** [14][16], **AgentBoard**, and **ToolEmu** received descriptive confirmation only. A responsible adoption ranking is **not possible** from the evidence gathered; the report below documents what was confirmed, what could not be verified, and concrete remediation steps.

---

## 2. Key Papers

> Note: The papers below are the ones actually returned during evidence collection. Several are foundational/survey works rather than tool-use benchmarks specifically; the tool-use benchmark papers named in the brief (API-Bank, ToolBench, ToolLLM, WebArena, Mind2Web, WebShop, SWE-bench, GAIA, etc.) **could not be verified as primary sources** and are therefore not listed here.

**Surveys on LLM agents and evaluation**
- *A survey on large language model based autonomous agents* (2024) — Widely cited survey (reported ~1672×) framing autonomous LLM agent architectures and evaluation. [3] — https://doi.org/10.1007/s11704-024-40231-1
- *A Survey on RAG Meeting LLMs: Towards Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models* (2024) — Survey connecting RAG pipelines to LLM agent tool-use contexts. [9] — https://doi.org/10.1145/3637528.3671470
- *Recent Advances in Natural Language Processing via Large Pre-trained Language Models: A Survey* (2023) — Background on pretrained LMs underpinning agent tool use. [5] — https://doi.org/10.1145/3605943
- *A Comprehensive Overview of Large Language Models* (2023) — Broad LLM overview including tool-augmentation context. [10] — https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2307.06435
- *A Review on Large Language Models: Architectures, Applications, Taxonomies, Open Issues and Challenges* (2024) — Taxonomy-level review of LLM capabilities. [7] — https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2024.3365742

**Adjacent / domain-specific works returned**
- *Can Open Large Language Models Catch Vulnerabilities?* (2025) — Empirical LLM evaluation in a security domain. [8] — https://doi.org/10.4230/oasics.icpec.2025.4
- *Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition* (1998) — Foundational CNN reference (LeNet). [1] — https://doi.org/10.1109/5.726791
- *SciPy 1.0: fundamental algorithms for scientific computing in Python* (2020) — Scientific-computing tooling often invoked by agents. [4] — https://doi.org/10.1038/s41592-019-0686-2
- *LAMMPS - a flexible simulation tool for particle-based materials modeling at the atomic, meso, and continuum scales* (2021) — Simulation tool relevant to scientific agent tool use. [2] — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpc.2021.108171
- *Advanced capabilities for materials modelling with Quantum ESPRESSO* (2017) — Materials-science tooling. [6] — https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-648x/aa8f79
- *fastp: an ultra-fast all-in-one FASTQ preprocessor* (2018) — Bioinformatics tool. [11] — https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/bty560
- *DnaSP 6: DNA Sequence Polymorphism Analysis of Large Data Sets* (2017) — Bioinformatics tool. [12] — https://doi.org/10.1093/molbev/msx248

**Benchmarks confirmed descriptively (no primary source retrieved)**
- **BFCL (Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard)** — Only benchmark with verified live adoption: active leaderboard (V4), integrated into UK AISI's Inspect Evals.
- **AgentBench** — Described as the first LLM-as-Agent benchmark spanning diverse interactive environments. [14][16]
- **AgentBoard** — Multi-turn interactive tool environments with fine-grained progress metrics.
- **ToolEmu** — Safety-focused; 36 high-stakes tools, 144 test cases.
- **VisualWebArena** (2024), **WebVoyager** (2024), **WebWalker** (2025) — Web/GUI agent evaluation.
- **TheAgentCompany** (2025) — Embodied/OS-style agent tasks.

**Named in the brief but NOT verified as primary sources:** API-Bank, ToolBench, ToolAlpaca, ToolLLM, APIBench, WebArena, Mind2Web, WebShop, MiniWoB++, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, OSWorld, SWE-bench, GAIA.

---

## 3. Datasets

Only Hugging Face datasets were retrieved; none are canonical tool-use benchmarks, and no download/like metadata was obtained.

- `fireworks-ai/function-calling-eval-dataset-v0` — https://huggingface.co/datasets/fireworks-ai/function-calling-eval-dataset-v0
- `Saxo/alpaca_function_calling_dataset` — https://huggingface.co/datasets/Saxo/alpaca_function_calling_dataset
- `Johin/function-calling-dataset` — https://huggingface.co/datasets/Johin/function-calling-dataset
- `DeepNLP/Agent-Function-Calling-Open-Dataset` — https://huggingface.co/datasets/DeepNLP/Agent-Function-Calling-Open-Dataset
- `DataPilot/Function-Calling-Japanese-Dataset` — https://huggingface.co/datasets/DataPilot/Function-Calling-Japanese-Dataset

**Caveat:** These are function-calling *training/eval* datasets, not agentic tool-use *benchmarks*. They should not be conflated with BFCL, AgentBench [14][16], AgentBoard, or ToolEmu.

---

## 4. Suggested Next Steps

1. **Re-run arXiv and Semantic Scholar with exponential backoff and rotating user agents.** The 429/503 failures were the single largest blocker; a retry pass with rate-limit-aware scheduling should recover primary sources for API-Bank, ToolBench, ToolLLM, WebArena, Mind2Web, WebShop, SWE-bench, GAIA, and OSWorld.
2. **Query OpenAlex by exact title for each named benchmark.** OpenAlex provides stable, citable metadata (including citation counts) and is not subject to the same rate-limit failures observed on arXiv/S2.
3. **Pull Hugging Face download/like metadata and Papers with Code leaderboards programmatically.** This is the only defensible way to produce an adoption/usage ranking; without these signals, any ranking would be unsupported.
4. **Cross-check BFCL V4 and Inspect Evals directly.** Since BFCL is the sole benchmark with verified live adoption, treat it as the anchor and use it to calibrate the credibility of any other benchmark claims surfaced in step 1–3.

**Bottom line:** Do not publish an adoption ranking until steps 1–3 are completed. The current evidence base supports only a *qualitative* map of the tool-use benchmark landscape, anchored on BFCL.

# LoRA vs QLoRA for Fine-Tuning LLMs under ~8GB VRAM
### A Research Report

---

## 1. TL;DR

For fine-tuning 7–8B parameter LLMs on a single ~8GB GPU, **QLoRA is effectively the only viable option**: it combines a 4-bit NF4 quantized base model with LoRA adapters and fits in ~5–8GB VRAM, whereas standard LoRA typically requires ~12GB+ and full fine-tuning 28GB+ [1][16][18]. The anchor paper (Dettmers et al., 2023) reports QLoRA matches 16-bit full fine-tuning quality on high-quality small datasets at rank 64 [1], though independent 8GB-specific head-to-head benchmarks remain scarce and most practical claims come from vendor/blog sources rather than peer-reviewed studies [16][18][19][20].

---

## 2. Key Papers

- **QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs (2023)** — The foundational paper; introduces 4-bit NF4 quantization + double quantization + paged optimizers, showing QLoRA matches 16-bit full FT quality with rank 64 on small high-quality datasets [1]. — https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2305.14314

- **A Survey on LoRA of Large Language Models (2024)** — Comprehensive survey of LoRA variants, applications, and tradeoffs across the LLM fine-tuning landscape [2]. — https://doi.org/10.1007/s11704-024-40663-9

- **Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Large Models: A Comprehensive Survey (2024)** — Broad PEFT survey covering LoRA, QLoRA, adapters, and related methods with memory/quality comparisons [6]. — https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2403.14608

- **Scaling Down to Scale Up: A Guide to Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (2023)** — Practical guide comparing PEFT methods including LoRA and QLoRA on efficiency and quality axes [7]. — https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2303.15647

- **Machine Translation with Large Language Models: Prompting, Few-shot Learning, and Fine-tuning with QLoRA (2023)** — Empirical QLoRA study on MT tasks; demonstrates quality retention under 4-bit quantization [4]. — https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2023.wmt-1.43

- **Fine-Tuning Large Language Models for Specialized Use Cases (2024)** — Applied study of LoRA/QLoRA for domain adaptation, with practical guidance on hyperparameters and memory [3]. — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mcpdig.2024.11.005

- **Fine-tuning large language models for chemical text mining (2024)** — Domain-specific QLoRA application showing quality parity with full FT on specialized corpora [5]. — https://doi.org/10.1039/d4sc00924j

- **LoftQ: LoRA-Fine-Tuning-Aware Quantization for Large Language Models (2023)** — Improves on QLoRA by jointly optimizing quantization and LoRA initialization; relevant when quality gaps appear [10]. — https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2310.08659

- **Memory-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Compressed Large Language Models via sub-4-bit Integer Quantization (2023)** — Explores sub-4-bit quantization for further VRAM reduction beyond QLoRA [11]. — https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2305.14152

- **OWQ: Outlier-Aware Weight Quantization for Efficient Fine-Tuning and Inference of Large Language Models (2024)** — Addresses outlier weights that degrade 4-bit quality; complementary to QLoRA [9]. — https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v38i12.29237

- **LoRAPrune: Structured Pruning Meets Low-Rank Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (2024)** — Combines pruning with LoRA to further reduce memory footprint [12]. — https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2024.findings-acl.178

- **A fine-tuning enhanced RAG system with quantized influence measure as AI judge (2024)** — Applied QLoRA + RAG pipeline; useful as a systems-level reference [8]. — https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-79110-x

---

## 3. Datasets

One dataset was retrieved during this survey: a LoRA/QLoRA benchmark dataset hosted on Hugging Face [13]. The remaining literature reviewed is methodological (quantization/PEFT techniques) rather than dataset-centric, so this is expected. For hands-on benchmarking, standard candidates would be Alpaca, Dolly-15k, or OpenAssistant — but these were **not** surfaced by the search and should be treated as suggestions, not findings.

---

## 4. Suggested Next Steps

1. **Run a controlled 8GB head-to-head benchmark.** The literature gap is real: no peer-reviewed source directly benchmarks LoRA vs QLoRA on an 8GB GPU [1][16][18]. Fine-tune the same 7–8B model (e.g., Llama-3-8B or Mistral-7B) with identical data/hyperparameters under (a) QLoRA 4-bit NF4 and (b) LoRA 16-bit, measuring task accuracy, perplexity, peak VRAM, and wall-clock time. This would be a genuinely novel contribution.

2. **Test LoftQ and OWQ as QLoRA upgrades.** Both papers directly target the quality loss from naive 4-bit quantization [10][9]. If your QLoRA results underperform, LoftQ's quantization-aware LoRA initialization is the most promising drop-in improvement [10].

3. **Benchmark tooling stacks on the same task.** Unsloth, Axolotl, LLaMA-Factory, and vanilla PEFT+bitsandbytes+TRL all claim different speed/VRAM profiles [17]. A single reproducible config across all four would clarify the "~2× faster, ~70% less VRAM" Unsloth claim, which is currently vendor-sourced only [17].

4. **Validate the "rank 64 is sufficient" claim on your domain.** Dettmers et al.'s rank recommendation was established on small high-quality datasets [1]. For specialized domains (chemistry, MT, legal), sweep r ∈ {8, 16, 32, 64, 128} under QLoRA to confirm the optimum before committing to a production config [1][4][5].

---

**Caveats:** arXiv and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited (HTTP 429) during retrieval, so coverage is incomplete. Most quantitative memory/speed claims (especially Unsloth's) are vendor- or blog-sourced rather than peer-reviewed [16][17][18][19][20]. No retrieved source directly benchmarked an 8GB GPU; the "~5–8GB for 7–8B QLoRA" figure is an extrapolation from the QLoRA paper's memory analysis and community reports, and should be verified empirically before relying on it [1][16][18].

## 1. TL;DR

Practitioner consensus in 2025–2026 points to **Qdrant, Milvus, and Weaviate** as the leading open-source vector databases for RAG, with **pgvector, Chroma, and LanceDB** serving lighter-weight or Postgres-native use cases [11][12][13][14][16]. The dominant selection drivers are **filtered-search speed, scalability, hybrid search, quantization/GPU support, ops cost, and framework integration** [9][10][11][12] — but the evidence base here is secondary (engineering blogs, surveys) and **no quantitative benchmark data was successfully retrieved**, so these preferences should be treated as directional rather than robust [11][12].

## 4. Synthesis (Practitioner Preferences)

**Consensus leaders:** Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate — with pgvector, Chroma, LanceDB as lighter-weight alternatives [11][12][13][14][16].

| DB | Practitioner positioning | Primary driver |
|---|---|---|
| **Qdrant** | "Production default" (Rust, low overhead, pre-filter payload search) [14][16] | Filtered-search speed [11][12] |
| **Milvus** | Billion-scale deployments [13] | Scalability [11][12] |
| **Weaviate** | Hybrid search, AI-native / knowledge-graph features [7][11] | Hybrid + ecosystem [11] |
| **pgvector** | Teams already on Postgres [11] | Avoid second service [11] |
| **Chroma** | Local dev / demos [11] | DX; struggles at production scale [11] |
| **LanceDB** | Embedded / columnar workloads [11] | Lightweight ops [11] |

**Selection drivers (ranked by frequency in sources):**
1. Filtered-search speed (pre-filter vs post-filter) [9][10][11][12]
2. Scalability (10M → 1B+ vectors) [10][11][12][13]
3. Hybrid search (dense + sparse/BM25) [9][11]
4. Quantization / GPU support [10][11][12]
5. Ops cost (managed vs self-hosted, memory footprint) [11][12][14]
6. Framework integration (LangChain / LlamaIndex / Haystack all support the same set) [9][19]

**Named papers referenced in the brief (not all retrieved with links):** Gao et al. *RAG for LLMs: A Survey* (2023); *A Survey on RAG Meeting LLMs* (2024); *Evaluation of RAG: A Survey* (2025); *Agentic RAG: A Survey* (arXiv 2501.09136); *Multi-Meta-RAG* (2025, metadata filtering); *TigerVector* (2025, graph+vector) [9][10].

## 5. Critical Caveats

- **No quantitative benchmark data was recovered.** arXiv and Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 429 during the run; ANN-Benchmarks and VectorDBBench results were never captured [11][12]. All performance claims above are **blog-level and unverified** [11][12].
- **No primary HN/Reddit threads** were obtained, so "practitioner consensus" is inferred from secondary write-ups rather than raw discussion [11][12].
- **No GitHub community-health metrics** (stars, issue velocity, release cadence, contributor counts) were collected [11][12].
- **The integration-depth → preference link is unverified** [9][19].
- Several "key papers" listed are **off-domain** (protein fitness, sign language, intrusion detection) and should be excluded from any downstream citation of this report [1][4][5][6][8].

**Bottom line:** Directional consensus favors Qdrant / Milvus / Weaviate, but the evidence base is secondary and qualitative [11][12]. Do not treat these preferences as robust until the gaps below are closed.

## 6. Suggested Next Steps

1. **Re-run rate-limited academic searches with backoff/API keys.** Target arXiv (2402.01763, 2310.14021, 2608.12812) and Semantic Scholar for the RAG-survey cluster (Gao 2023; RAG-Meets-LLMs 2024; RAG Evaluation 2025; Agentic RAG 2501.09136; Multi-Meta-RAG; TigerVector). Capture abstracts + citation counts to replace the missing quantitative layer [9][10][11][12].
2. **Directly scrape ANN-Benchmarks and VectorDBBench repos.** Pull the latest result JSONs and reproduce the filtered-search (15–25% selectivity) and 100M-vector claims attributed to Qdrant; publish the raw numbers rather than blog summaries [11][12][14][16].
3. **Mine primary practitioner threads.** Query the HN Algolia API and Reddit (`r/LocalLLaMA`, `r/MachineLearning`, `r/vectordatabase`) for 2025–2026 threads mentioning each DB; code comments by driver (latency, recall, filtering, ops cost, ecosystem) to test the ranked driver list empirically [11][12].
4. **Collect GitHub community-health metrics.** For Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate, pgvector, Chroma, LanceDB: stars, commit cadence, open/closed issue ratio, median time-to-close, release frequency, and contributor concentration — then correlate with the preference ranking to test whether ecosystem health predicts practitioner choice [11][12][13][14][16].
5. **Run a controlled filtered-search benchmark.** Fix embedding model, dataset (e.g., a public 100M-scale set), and selectivity sweep (1%, 5%, 15%, 25%); measure p50/p99 latency, recall@10, and RAM/disk per DB. This is the single highest-value artifact missing from the current evidence base [11][12].
